$comment: The representation rules: which way of showing a collection fits which task and data shape. A zone that declares its task and data shape may only name a representation some matching rule chooses; spec-selection.mjs enforces it. The division of labour is deliberate — the spec author names the task and the data, which is a judgment a reviewer approves; this file decides what that judgment permits, which is a computation. Adapted from css's screen-specs/selection-rules.json to harness's role vocabulary: harness names three collection representations (table, list, cards → the roles table, list, card) and does not yet have roles for a virtualized grid or for stat tiles, so the css rules that select 'grid' (R2) or 'stats' (R5, R6) and the hard constraints that send you to a grid (H1 unbounded, H2 editable) are reduced to what this vocabulary can express, and noted where dropped. Sources: NN/g (data tables, cards, dashboards), uxpatterns.dev, Smart Interface Design Patterns, SAP Fiori floorplans.

table.means: columns over rows: side-by-side comparison, sort and filter by field

list.means: one row per item, few attributes, linear scanning

cards.means: self-contained tiles: each item read and judged on its own

rules.title: Looking up and comparing records wants columns
rules.because: Two adjacent data points in a column are compared without moving the eyes or holding values in working memory; cards force spatial reorientation per item and de-emphasize ranking (NN/g data tables, NN/g cards).
rules.good: a table with sortable columns, one row per record
rules.bad: a card per record with ten meta rows — comparing two records now means reading two paragraphs

rules.title: Scanning a few attributes wants rows
rules.because: With one to three attributes per item a linear list scans fastest; columns earn their chrome only when several fields are compared (uxpatterns.dev: start with list).
rules.good: a list item: title, one meta line, a trailing action
rules.bad: a three-column table whose header row labels the obvious

rules.title: Judging candidates one by one wants tiles
rules.because: Browsing has no single target: each item is read and judged on its own content, so it gets a self-contained surface. The moment the job becomes comparing fields across items, the task is compare and R1 applies (NN/g cards: browsing, not searching).
rules.good: a card per candidate: name, a status tag, the reasons as sentences
rules.bad: a table whose cells hold sentences — comparison across rows of prose compares nothing

rules.title: Prose is never tabular
rules.because: A collection of text-heavy items (questions, messages, findings) is read item by item; a table of paragraphs has columns that align nothing (NN/g data tables: tables are for discrete comparable values).
rules.good: a card per question: who asked, the text, the answer, the actions
rules.bad: a table with a 'Question' column four lines tall

rules.title: A queue is a worklist
rules.because: Working through items that each need a decision is a worklist: the set is given, so it needs density and status, not discovery chrome (SAP Fiori worklist = list report minus the filter bar).
rules.good: a table of items with a status tag and one action per row
rules.bad: a card grid the user has to graze over to find what is next

rules.title: A short queue reads as cards
rules.because: R8's density argument is about SCALE: with a handful of items, per-item actions and reading beat column density. At cardinality many, R8 alone applies and cards fail again.
rules.good: a card per item: eyebrow, title, meta, two small actions
rules.bad: a three-row table whose header chrome outweighs its rows

rules.title: Entry points are tiles
rules.because: A hub's items are destinations, not records: a tile per destination with what is waiting inside it (SAP Fiori overview page).
rules.good: a card per destination: topic, what is waiting, when it arrived
rules.bad: a table of destinations with sortable columns nobody sorts

notes.say: three fields rarely earn columns — a list scans faster (uxpatterns.dev); keep the table only if column sorting is really used
